changes.text: 阿波马托克斯的受降条件里，军官的佩刀和私马私物都不是谈出来的——是格兰特写条文时自行加进去的；士兵的马骡则是李问起后，格兰特先答以按条文不行，李重读条款表示明白，格兰特随后主动口头准许的，没有写进条文。

At Appomattox, the officers' side-arms and their private horses and effects were never negotiated: Grant wrote them into the terms on his own, partway through the draft. When Lee asked about the soldiers' own horses and mules, Grant first answered that as written the terms did not allow it; Lee reread the terms and said that was clear, and Grant then offered on his own, verbally and without writing it into the terms, to let the men take the animals home.
8日，格兰特跟着在李军后方的波托马克军行进，正犯着重头痛，在路边一处离大部队有一段距离的农舍过夜，把脚泡进热水和芥末，手腕和后颈贴上芥末膏，指望天亮就能好。李来信提议会面，但按格兰特的说法，会面的目的并不是交出军队。格兰特的回信很干脆：他无权谈和，这样的会面不可能有好结果；和平的条件众所周知，南方只要放下武器，就能让和平早点到来，救下成千上万条人命和数以亿计尚未被毁的财产。

On the 8th Grant followed the Army of the Potomac, which was in rear of Lee, in the grip of a sick headache. He spent the night at a farmhouse on the road, some distance behind the main body of the army, bathing his feet in hot water and mustard and putting mustard plasters on his wrists and the back of his neck, hoping that by morning he would be cured. A letter from Lee proposed a meeting, but, as Grant tells it, for a different purpose from that of surrendering his army. Grant's answer was brisk. He had no authority to treat on the subject of peace, and the proposed meeting could lead to no good. The terms on which peace could be had, he wrote, were well understood: let the South lay down its arms, and the most desirable event would come sooner, sparing thousands of lives and hundreds of millions of property not yet destroyed.
作者认为，难处在于具体的受降条文得由他自己当场起草。基本条件已见于格兰特8日的信，李说自己就是这样理解的；但李要的是格兰特开出的条件，条文得由格兰特落笔写成。格兰特最后写下的那份条款里，有两处是落笔之后才想起来加进去的：军官的佩刀，以及军官的私马和私物。南军士兵自己的马骡则根本不在条文里：李问起时，格兰特先答以按条文不行，李表示明白，格兰特随后主动口头准许。

In the writer's view, the difficulty was that the actual terms of surrender were his to draft on the spot. The basic conditions had already appeared in Grant's letter of the 8th, and Lee said he had so understood it; but Lee had asked for the terms Grant proposed, and the written clauses were Grant's to set down. Two items in the terms he finally set down were afterthoughts, added only once his pen was already moving: the officers' side-arms, and the officers' private horses and effects. The horses and mules belonging to the Confederate enlisted men were not in the written terms at all: when Lee asked, Grant first answered that as written they could not be kept; Lee said that was clear, and Grant then offered on his own, verbally, to let the men take them home.

格兰特回信说，他没有谈和的权限，南方放下武器就能让和平早日到来。此后李再次来信，可这封信送得很费劲：由于格兰特所走的路线，这封信很可能无法在约定时间内送到他手里并带回答复，除非信使穿过南军战线。因此，李派人护送带信的军官穿过自己的战线，把信送到格兰特手里。另据格兰特记述，米德和谢里登都对是否停火非常犹豫，怕这不是真心求和；而且北弗吉尼亚军团已无路可逃，除非用诡计脱身。不过他们最终同意停火两小时，以便在这段时间里设法与格兰特联络。

Grant replied that he had no authority to treat on the subject of peace, and that by laying down their arms the South would hasten peace. Lee then wrote again, but this message was hard to deliver: from the route Grant had taken, it would probably not be possible to reach him and get an answer back within the time fixed unless the messenger passed through the rebel lines. Lee therefore sent an escort with the officer bearing the message through his own lines to Grant. Separately, Grant records that Meade and Sheridan both hesitated very considerably about suspending hostilities at all. They were afraid the overture was not in good faith; and the Army of Northern Virginia was where it could not escape except by some deception. They finally consented, however, to a suspension of hostilities for two hours, to give an opportunity of communicating with Grant in that time if possible.

接着李又说，他们的军队编制和联邦军不太一样（格兰特注意到，这话仍暗指双方是两个国家），骑兵和炮兵的马是自备的，问这些人能不能把马带走。格兰特回答，按写好的条文不行，只有军官可以带走私物。李把条款又读了一遍，说这很清楚。格兰特接着讲了一段：他估计这大概是这场战争的最后一仗，他真心希望如此；据他看来，士兵多半是小农，地方已被两军搜掠殆尽，没有手边的马，恐怕种不出养活一家人过冬的收成。美国不需要这些牲口，所以他要交代留守受降的军官：凡自称有马或骡的南军士兵，都可以把牲口牵回家。李再次说，这会产生良好影响。

Then Lee remarked that their army was organized a little differently from that of the United States — still implying, Grant noted, that they were two countries — and that in their army the cavalrymen and artillerists owned their own horses. Was he to understand that the men who owned their horses could keep them? As the terms stood, Grant said, they could not; only the officers were permitted to take their private property. Lee read over the terms a second time and remarked that that was clear. Grant then went on. He thought this would be about the last battle of the war, and sincerely hoped so. He took it that most of the men in the ranks were small farmers, and the whole country had been so raided by the two armies that it was doubtful whether they could put in a crop to carry themselves and their families through the next winter without the horses they were riding. The United States did not want the animals, and he would therefore instruct the officers he left behind, while taking the paroles of Lee's troops, to let every man of the Confederate army who claimed to own a horse or mule take the animal home. Lee remarked again that this would have a happy effect.

李写信接受条件，说条款与格兰特8日来信中所提的实质相同，他将指定军官来办交接。在告辞之前，他说自己的军队状况很糟：缺粮，没有草料，士兵连日只吃炒玉米，需要请格兰特供应口粮和草料。格兰特说当然可以，问需要多少人的口粮，李答约两万五千人；格兰特便让李派自己的军需官和军需主任到两三英里外的阿波马托克斯车站，从被截停的列车上取用所需。格兰特指定吉本、格里芬、梅里特三位将军负责在李的部队回乡前办理宣誓遣散，李留下朗斯特里特、戈登、彭德尔顿三位将军与他们协商，以便利此事。两人随后像见面时一样友好地分别，李回到自己的战线。李走后不久，格兰特给陆军部长斯坦顿发电报，说李已于当天下午按他提出的条件交出北弗吉尼亚军团。

Lee wrote accepting the terms: being substantially the same as those expressed in Grant's letter of the 8th, they were accepted, and he would designate the proper officers to carry the stipulations into effect. Before taking his leave he added that his army was in a very bad condition for want of food, and without forage; his men had been living for days on parched corn exclusively, and he would have to ask Grant for rations and forage. Grant agreed at once and asked how many men needed rations; about twenty-five thousand, Lee answered. Grant authorized him to send his own commissary and quartermaster to Appomattox Station, two or three miles away, where out of the trains the Union had stopped they could have all the provisions wanted. Grant designated Generals Gibbon, Griffin and Merritt to carry into effect the paroling of Lee's troops before they started for their homes, and Lee left Generals Longstreet, Gordon and Pendleton for them to confer with in order to facilitate the work. The two men then separated as cordially as they had met, Lee returning to his own lines. Soon after Lee's departure Grant telegraphed Secretary of War Stanton that Lee had surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia that afternoon on terms proposed by Grant himself.
马骡的宽许不在已写成的条文里，是格兰特当面对李承诺、将指示留守军官办理的。格兰特记下由吉本、格里芬、梅里特负责宣誓遣散，李留下朗斯特里特、戈登、彭德尔顿与之协商；但本章没有写宣誓遣散和马骡宽许的实际执行经过。日期大多按原文「the 8th」这样的写法转述；原文所录电报注明的日期是1865年4月9日。

The indulgence on horses and mules was not in the terms as written; Grant promised Lee he would instruct the officers left behind to allow it. Grant records that Gibbon, Griffin and Merritt were designated to carry out the paroling, with Lee leaving Longstreet, Gordon and Pendleton for them to confer with; but this chapter does not describe how the paroling or the horse-and-mule allowance was actually carried out. Dates are mostly kept as the source has them — "the 8th" and the like; the telegraph the source reproduces is dated April 9th, 1865.
全文只有一个史源，即格兰特本人的回忆记述。对话是他的转述，未必逐字；他明言不知李的心情；本文不替任何一方补写心理；马匹宽许不在已写成的条文中，是格兰特当面答应李将指示留守军官办理的，其落实情况原文没有交代；原文记有宣誓遣散的执行人员安排，但未写执行经过；日期大多按原文写法转述，原文所录电报注明1865年4月9日。

There is only one source for this piece: Grant's own account in his memoirs. The conversations are his retellings and need not be verbatim; he says expressly that he did not know Lee's feelings, and this piece does not supply psychology for either side; the allowance on horses and mules was not in the written terms but promised to Lee as an instruction to the officers left behind, and its implementation is not reported; the source records who was assigned to carry out the paroling, but not how it was carried out; dates are mostly kept in the original wording, and the telegraph the source reproduces is dated April 9th, 1865.
